# Dash Essential Dash Essential is a native hardware-control application for Xiaomi Dash (POCO X8 Pro Max / Redmi Turbo 5 Max) and its MediaTek Dimensity 9500s (MT6991) platform. It combines an Android `NativeActivity`, a Flutter AOT interface, a Rust host runtime, and a separately privileged Rust daemon. The UI and hardware-control logic remain native/AOT. A small, framework-only DEX adapter provides the Quick Settings bypass tile and Android predictive Back callbacks; it contains no AndroidX, Compose or third-party managed libraries. The APK never runs as root, does not use the system UID, and does not request privileged Android permissions. Kernel and vendor controls are owned by the daemon and reached through authenticated local transports restricted to the installed application UID. ## Supported target - Device codename: `dash` - SoC: MediaTek MT6991 / Dimensity 9500s - CPU: 8 cores (4× Cortex-A720 + 3× Cortex-X4 + 1× Cortex-X925), 4+3+1 policies, up to 3.73 GHz - GPU: Arm Immortalis-G925, 12 cores, up to 1612 MHz - ABI: ARM64 - Android: API 31 or newer - Kernel userspace: 16 KB page-compatible native binaries - Vendor dependencies: Dash touch and display AIDL services plus MediaTek GED This is device-specific software. Other devices are rejected by the root-module installer and are not supported by the included AOSP policy. ## Main features - Four persistent GPU performance profiles with live hardware readback. - Mali devfreq range, governor, GED boost, power-policy, and OPP controls. - CPU core mask, independent cluster governors, and validated per-cluster minimum/maximum or sustained exact-lock controls sourced from the live kernel OPP table. - UFS scheduler selection across every detected UFS logical unit. - Touch profiles for 240 Hz native timing, 480 Hz native timing, and the original v1.18.0 one-millisecond Android output stream generated from the native 480 Hz source. - Xiaomi touch/display AIDL integration, color modes, expert calibration, sunlight mode, HDR/video controls, resolution, and density controls. - ZRAM size, algorithm, swappiness, compaction, charging, and power telemetry. - Kernel-supported bypass charging with Immediate or 20/40/80/90% thresholds, daemon-owned persistence and measured battery-flow reporting. - Whole-app hardware-control pause and reset, plus OEM Control defaults for touch response and display colour/temperature. - [System Colors](docs/SYSTEM_COLORS.md): Android Material You seed palettes, wallpaper reset, style previews, and capability-based native color readback without a HyperOS, ColorOS, or AOSP ROM-name allowlist. - Daemon-owned persistence and background reassertion after boot, screen wake, vendor resets, app force-close, or removal from recents. - Configurable in-app motion timing with native 120 Hz frame pacing. - [Per-App Controls](docs/PER_APP_CONTROLS_IMPLEMENTATION.md): foreground touch, refresh-rate, CPU and GPU overrides, with saved profiles and global/ROM restoration. Starts disabled; system apps are hidden by default. - [Memory DVFS & UFS](docs/MEMORY_STORAGE_TRIALS.md): supported dynamic ranges, exact driver-policy requests and OEM Reset. These are session controls, recovered to originals after daemon restart or reboot. - Bypass Charging Quick Settings/Control Center tile with direct access to Charging Control on long-press. ## Screenshots The redesigned interface groups live device telemetry and hardware tuning into focused panels for each subsystem.

Home - Device Pulse and quick controls
Control Hubs - Hardware subsystem navigation
CPU - Core and frequency control
GPU - Mali profiles and GED

Touch - Response profiles
Display - Color and HDR tuning
Battery - Charging telemetry
ZRAM - Memory compression

Diagnostics - Runtime health checks
Support - Community and safety information
System Colors - Material You palette control
Advanced Configuration - CPU governors and device tuning

Resolution - Canvas, density, and refresh settings
Additional Screen 1 - Device configuration
Additional Screen 2 - Device configuration
System Colors - Updated palette controls
## Performance profiles | Profile | GPU range and governor | GED / power policy | CPU behavior | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Stock Balanced | Vendor-managed 338–1612 MHz, `dummy` | GED off, `coarse_demand` | Unchanged; controlled separately | | Gaming Dynamic | 338–1612 MHz, `simple_ondemand` | GED on, `always_on` | Unchanged; controlled separately | | Battery Saver | 338–598 MHz, `powersave` | GED off, `coarse_demand` | Unchanged; controlled separately | | Extreme Beast | Fixed 1612 MHz, `performance`, DVFS off | GED on, `always_on` | Unchanged; controlled separately | GPU profiles never modify CPU governors, CPU clock ranges, or CPU core state. Vendor CPU and platform thermal services remain running in every mode. Gaming Dynamic and Extreme Beast override the Mali cooling constraint and can still cause extreme heat, rapid battery drain, instability, or an emergency hardware shutdown. Custom CPU ranges remain separate from GPU profiles and governors. While at least one custom CPU range is active, the daemon selects Dash's OEM `thermal-nolimits` configuration so Xiaomi's userspace policy cannot replace an exact lock with a lower ceiling. It keeps the thermal services alive, remembers the configuration that was active beforehand, and restores it when the final custom CPU range is reset. Gaming Dynamic and Extreme Beast borrow the vendor's `thermal_ap` configuration instead of the `thermal-nolimits` mode CPU ranges use. The borrow is disabled by default (`MI_THERMAL_AP_MODE = -1`); enable it after on-device verification by setting the mode id. GPU thermal borrow applies only when no CPU range is saved — CPU range ownership holds the stricter `nolimits` mode, which takes precedence. A background guard self-heals a stuck `sconfig=6` (nolimits) left by a daemon restart or a lost save: when no saved range or thermal mode owner exists and the live mode reads `6`, it immediately writes `0` (normal) and logs a warning. ## Integration choices | Method | APK privilege | Backend | Persistence | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | AOSP ROM integration | Normal app UID | Root init daemon | `/data/system/dash-essential/state.conf` | | KernelSU Next or Magisk | Normal app UID | Root module daemon | `/data/adb/dash-essential/state.conf` | | Standalone APK | Normal app UID | None | Hardware controls unavailable | For a ROM release, use the AOSP integration. It installs the APK and daemon in `/product`, creates a dedicated app SELinux domain, restricts the control socket to that domain, starts the daemon after boot, and restores saved state without a root manager. See [AOSP ROM integration](docs/ROM_INTEGRATION.md) for the complete maintainer workflow and [Architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) for runtime details. ## Build from source Required tools: - Linux host - Flutter SDK and revision-matched Flutter engine checkout - Rust toolchain with `aarch64-linux-android` - Android SDK, platform 36, build-tools, and NDK r27 or newer - JDK 17 or newer, `ninja`, `zip`, `unzip`, and standard ELF tools Build the pinned engine once: ```bash rustup target add aarch64-linux-android ./tools/build-flutter-engine.sh ``` Build without touching a connected device: ```bash DASH_BUILD_ONLY=1 ./build-and-install.sh ``` Output is written under `out/release//`. The build verifies Flutter analysis, ARM64 AOT output, the restricted platform DEX adapter, APK signing, 16 KB ZIP alignment, 16 KB ELF segment alignment, and a content stamp covering the packaged Flutter assets and ICU data. If no signing key is supplied, a stable development key is created once under the ignored `out/signing/` directory and reused by later local builds. For release signing, set: ```bash DASH_KEYSTORE=/absolute/path/release.jks \ DASH_KEY_ALIAS=release \ DASH_KEYSTORE_PASS='store-password' \ DASH_KEY_PASS='key-password' \ DASH_BUILD_ONLY=1 ./build-and-install.sh ``` ## Export for an AOSP tree ```bash DASH_KEYSTORE=/absolute/path/rom-app.jks \ DASH_KEY_ALIAS=dash-essential \ DASH_KEYSTORE_PASS='store-password' \ DASH_KEY_PASS='key-password' \ ./tools/export-aosp-bundle.sh ``` The generated `dist/aosp/DashEssential-/` directory contains the APK, daemon, control client, `Android.bp`, init service, split product/vendor SELinux policy, the APK public certificate used by the dedicated app-domain mapping, and checksums. Keep the same private key for every ROM update; the private key is never copied into the bundle. To build, stage, and wire the integration into an existing ROM source tree in one command, provide the Dash product makefile and BoardConfig path: ```bash DASH_KEYSTORE=/absolute/path/rom-app.jks \ DASH_KEY_ALIAS=dash-essential \ DASH_KEYSTORE_PASS='store-password' \ DASH_KEY_PASS='key-password' \ ./tools/integrate-aosp-rom.sh /absolute/path/to/aosp \ device/xiaomi/dash/device.mk \ device/xiaomi/dash/BoardConfig.mk ``` The helper creates `vendor/dash-essential`, verifies the complete build, and adds the two exact include lines only when absent. It refuses paths outside the selected source tree and never replaces an existing integration directory. Passing only the AOSP root keeps the previous stage-only behavior. ## KernelSU Next and Magisk module For an existing rooted ROM, build the combined application and daemon module: ```bash DASH_KEYSTORE=/absolute/path/release.jks \ DASH_KEY_ALIAS=release \ DASH_KEYSTORE_PASS='store-password' \ DASH_KEY_PASS='key-password' \ ./tools/build-kernelsu-next-module.sh ``` Install the ZIP from KernelSU Next Manager or the Magisk app while Android is running. The installer registers the bundled APK as an ordinary user app and the module runs only the separate hardware daemon as root. No live SELinux patch, system overlay, privileged-app conversion, or app-to-root socket rule is used. The direct Unix transport uses `SO_PEERCRED`. ROMs that block cross-domain Unix `connectto` use a root-privileged localhost port instead; the app first proves from its own UID/SELinux context that low-port binding is denied, and the daemon resolves the accepted client's UID from `/proc/net/tcp` before serving a command. A daemon-initiated Unix path remains as a compatibility fallback. Module Action reports which authenticated transport completed instead of treating a root-only control-client ping as proof. The package uses `skip_mount`; because it overlays no partition files, KernelSU does not require a metamodule. Recovery installation is not supported. Keep the signing key for every future module update. Android rejects an APK update signed by a different certificate. The first release after the signing identity reset includes a one-time migration for module installations: it tries a normal update first and only removes/reinstalls the user application when Android reports a certificate mismatch. Hardware profiles stored under `/data/adb/dash-essential` remain intact, while application-local preferences reset once. Later releases signed by the retained key update normally. The same ZIP can also act as a temporary update layer over a ROM-native Dash Essential installation when that ROM APK uses the same signing certificate as the release APK. The installer updates the app without clearing its data, the module daemon reuses `/data/system/dash-essential`, and native init is stopped before the module daemon starts. Removing the module rolls the app back to the ROM copy and restarts the native service. A differently signed ROM build is rejected without uninstalling the app or deleting its data; that build must be updated through its maintainer's OTA or original signing key. ## Repository layout ```text android/ aosp/ AOSP prebuilt, init, and SELinux integration template kernelsu-next/ KernelSU Next and Magisk module source package/ Manifest and Android resources platform/ Minimal Android tile and Back callback adapters docs/ Architecture, build, and ROM maintainer documentation runtime/ daemon-rust/ Privileged hardware backend and control client flutter-engine/ Embedder header and ignored pinned engine prebuilts host-rust/ NativeActivity, Flutter embedder, JNI, and IPC bridge tools/ Engine, AOSP export, and module build scripts ui/flutter/ Flutter AOT interface ``` ## Documentation - [Architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) - [Building and verification](docs/BUILDING.md) - [AOSP ROM integration](docs/ROM_INTEGRATION.md) - [Unpacked EROFS/ext4 ROM integration](docs/UNPACKED_ROM_PORTER_GUIDE.md): Dash-only additions and a merge tool using the porter's own ROM policy. - [Flutter runtime pin](docs/FLUTTER_RUNTIME.md) - [Commit convention](docs/COMMITS.md) ## Port notes: Rodin Essential to Dash (MT6991) This tree is a port of [Rodin Essential](https://github.com/NEESCHAL-3/Rodin-Essential) by **NEESCHAL-3**, reworked for the MediaTek MT6991 `dash` platform by **afrizal1211**, and carried along the SaanOS line of the same project by **Saan**. The upstream release it is based on is `v1.18.5`. The upstream project's licence, copyright notice and release history are preserved; [NOTICE](NOTICE) lists the modifications. The port is tested on real hardware by the [@PocoX8ProMaxID](https://t.me/PocoX8ProMaxID) Telegram community. The port changed the following. Every value was taken from the shipped dash kernel, device tree and ROM rather than carried over from MT6899. ### The GPU ladder The upstream target's Mali-G720 published a uniformly spaced 26 MHz operating-point ladder, so an OPP index could be computed from a frequency with a formula. Dash's Immortalis-G925 does not: - The device tree publishes 52 operating points from 1612 MHz down to 338 MHz, and the three lowest entries all report the same 338 MHz. - The Mali devfreq node advertises 50 frequencies, while the GPUEB's own DVFS ladder has 52 slots. The same frequency therefore sits at a different index in each: 598 MHz is devfreq index 39 but GPUEB index 49, and 338 MHz is devfreq index 49 but GPUEB index 51. The daemon consequently resolves every operating-point index against the ladder the driver publishes at `/proc/gpufreqv2/gpu_working_opp_table`, and it publishes a floor and a ceiling the way MediaTek's own tooling does: `custom_boost_gpu_freq` carries the ladder position of the requested minimum, `custom_upbound_gpu_freq` the position of the requested maximum, and the `gpu_cust_boost_freq` / `gpu_cust_upbound_freq` parameters carry the frequencies themselves. A request the ladder cannot satisfy is reported as an error rather than written as a guessed index, because a wrong index moves the floor to an unrelated frequency. ### Device baselines | Item | Upstream target | Dash | | --- | --- | --- | | GPU devfreq | `13000000.mali` | `48000000.mali` | | GPU ladder | 260–1300 MHz, 41 uniform steps | 338–1612 MHz, 52 uneven steps | | Mali cooling device | fixed `cooling_device3` | resolved by type `devfreq-48000000.mali` | | UFS devfreq | `112b0000.ufshci` | `16810000.ufshci` | | DVFSRC devfreq | `/devices/platform/soc/1c00f000.dvfsrc/...` | `/devices/platform/1c013000.dvfsrc/...` | | Backlight | `/sys/class/backlight/panel0-backlight` | `/sys/class/leds/lcd-backlight` | | Native resolution | 1220 x 2712 | 1280 x 2772 | | Touch panel | Goodix / FocalTech | Novatek NT38771 | The CPU cluster layout is unchanged: Dash exposes the same 4+3+1 policy numbering (`policy0`, `policy4`, `policy7`) with eight cores. ### Thermal ownership Dash's thermal interface is the same one the upstream target used, including the `thermal_message/sconfig` configuration mode that suppresses the vendor's competing CPU policy while a custom CPU range is held. The vendor thermal services stay running in every mode. Gaming Dynamic and Extreme Beast borrow the vendor's `thermal_ap` configuration (mode `MI_THERMAL_AP_MODE`) instead of the `thermal-nolimits` mode CPU ranges use. The borrow is disabled by default (`MI_THERMAL_AP_MODE = -1`); enable it after on-device verification by setting the mode id. GPU thermal borrow applies only when no CPU range is saved — CPU range ownership holds the stricter `nolimits` mode, which takes precedence. The borrow is journaled via the service control journal and restored on release. A background guard self-heals a stuck `sconfig=6` (nolimits) left by a daemon restart or a lost save: when no saved range or thermal mode owner exists and the live mode reads `6`, it immediately writes `0` (normal) and logs a warning. The fresh-boot `-1` sentinel is normalized to `0` by `normalize_mi_thermal_config_mode`, so clean boots never false-trigger. ### The platform's GPU ceiling Dash's ladder has a plateau. Its 24 middle slots all report 1430 MHz, so a 1430 MHz floor resolves to the last of them and a 1430 MHz ceiling to the first, and both name the same clock. The MediaTek firmware's own `THERMAL_EB` row caps at the first of those slots, so the firmware's thermal ceiling is 1430 MHz even though the ladder's top operating point is 1612 MHz. That ceiling **cannot be raised from software.** The limit table the thermal framework arbitrates through is read-only on this ROM, and the platform's power service holds the GPU at or below 1430 MHz regardless. The app therefore reports the cap rather than fighting it: a profile whose own writes landed is shown as *armed and capped by THERMAL_EB*, with the effective ceiling read from the driver, and it is not re-applied on every tick. The effective ceiling is read twice, because the driver publishes it twice: as an index in the power policy status dump, and directly in hertz in `/sys/kernel/thermal/gpu_info`. The second form is simpler and does not need the status dump to be read whole. ### Known differences - Dash's stock kernel publishes no bypass-charging node, so the bypass-charging feature reports itself as unsupported rather than pretending to provide direct power. The charge-current limit is still available: dash exposes `constant_charge_current` on the battery power supply. - The charge-current tiers follow the upstream calibration. The absolute ceiling comes from the vendor charger configuration, which is not part of the public ROM dump, so it should be confirmed against the target hardware; the daemon verifies every write against its readback and reports a clamped or rejected value instead of pretending it applied. ## License Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

Dash Essential

Dash Essential is a native hardware-control application for Xiaomi Dash

(POCO X8 Pro Max / Redmi Turbo 5 Max) and its MediaTek Dimensity 9500s

(MT6991) platform.

It combines an Android NativeActivity, a Flutter AOT interface, a Rust host

runtime, and a separately privileged Rust daemon. The UI and hardware-control

logic remain native/AOT. A small, framework-only DEX adapter provides the

Quick Settings bypass tile and Android predictive Back callbacks; it contains

no AndroidX, Compose or third-party managed libraries.

The APK never runs as root, does not use the system UID, and does not request

privileged Android permissions. Kernel and vendor controls are owned by the

daemon and reached through authenticated local transports restricted to the

installed application UID.

Supported target

  • Device codename: `dash`
  • SoC: MediaTek MT6991 / Dimensity 9500s
  • CPU: 8 cores (4× Cortex-A720 + 3× Cortex-X4 + 1× Cortex-X925), 4+3+1

    • policies, up to 3.73 GHz

  • GPU: Arm Immortalis-G925, 12 cores, up to 1612 MHz
  • ABI: ARM64
  • Android: API 31 or newer
  • Kernel userspace: 16 KB page-compatible native binaries
  • Vendor dependencies: Dash touch and display AIDL services plus MediaTek GED

    • This is device-specific software. Other devices are rejected by the root-module

    installer and are not supported by the included AOSP policy.

    Main features

  • Four persistent GPU performance profiles with live hardware readback.
  • Mali devfreq range, governor, GED boost, power-policy, and OPP controls.
  • CPU core mask, independent cluster governors, and validated per-cluster

    • minimum/maximum or sustained exact-lock controls sourced from the live kernel

    OPP table.

  • UFS scheduler selection across every detected UFS logical unit.
  • Touch profiles for 240 Hz native timing, 480 Hz native timing, and the

    • original v1.18.0 one-millisecond Android output stream generated from the

    native 480 Hz source.

  • Xiaomi touch/display AIDL integration, color modes, expert calibration,

    • sunlight mode, HDR/video controls, resolution, and density controls.

  • ZRAM size, algorithm, swappiness, compaction, charging, and power telemetry.
  • Kernel-supported bypass charging with Immediate or 20/40/80/90% thresholds,

    • daemon-owned persistence and measured battery-flow reporting.

  • Whole-app hardware-control pause and reset, plus OEM Control defaults for

    • touch response and display colour/temperature.

  • [System Colors](docs/SYSTEM_COLORS.md): Android Material You seed palettes,

    • wallpaper reset, style previews, and capability-based native color readback

    without a HyperOS, ColorOS, or AOSP ROM-name allowlist.

  • Daemon-owned persistence and background reassertion after boot, screen wake,

    • vendor resets, app force-close, or removal from recents.

  • Configurable in-app motion timing with native 120 Hz frame pacing.
  • [Per-App Controls](docs/PER_APP_CONTROLS_IMPLEMENTATION.md): foreground touch,

    • refresh-rate, CPU and GPU overrides, with saved profiles and global/ROM

    restoration. Starts disabled; system apps are hidden by default.

  • [Memory DVFS & UFS](docs/MEMORY_STORAGE_TRIALS.md): supported dynamic ranges,

    • exact driver-policy requests and OEM Reset. These are session controls,

    recovered to originals after daemon restart or reboot.

  • Bypass Charging Quick Settings/Control Center tile with direct access to

    • Charging Control on long-press.

    Screenshots

    The redesigned interface groups live device telemetry and hardware tuning into

    focused panels for each subsystem.


    Home - Device Pulse and quick controls
    Control Hubs - Hardware subsystem navigation
    CPU - Core and frequency control
    GPU - Mali profiles and GED

    Performance profiles

    | Profile | GPU range and governor | GED / power policy | CPU behavior |

    | --- | --- | --- | --- |

    | Gaming Dynamic | 338–1612 MHz, simple_ondemand | GED on, always_on | Unchanged; controlled separately |

    | Battery Saver | 338–598 MHz, powersave | GED off, coarse_demand | Unchanged; controlled separately |

    | Extreme Beast | Fixed 1612 MHz, performance, DVFS off | GED on, always_on | Unchanged; controlled separately |

    GPU profiles never modify CPU governors, CPU clock ranges, or CPU core state.

    Vendor CPU and platform thermal services remain running in every mode. Gaming

    Dynamic and Extreme Beast override the Mali cooling constraint and can still

    cause extreme heat, rapid battery drain, instability, or an emergency hardware

    workflow and Architecture for runtime details.

  • Rust toolchain with `aarch64-linux-android`
  • Android SDK, platform 36, build-tools, and NDK r27 or newer
  • JDK 17 or newer, `ninja`, `zip`, `unzip`, and standard ELF tools

    rustup target add aarch64-linux-android
./tools/build-flutter-engine.sh

DASH_KEY_PASS='key-password' \

DASH_KEY_ALIAS=dash-essential \

    KernelSU Next and Magisk module

DASH_KEY_ALIAS=release \
DASH_KEYSTORE_PASS='store-password' \
DASH_KEY_PASS='key-password' \
  ./tools/build-kernelsu-next-module.sh

    The same ZIP can also act as a temporary update layer over a ROM-native Dash

    the release APK. The installer updates the app without clearing its data, the

    module daemon reuses /data/system/dash-essential, and native init is stopped

    before the module daemon starts. Removing the module rolls the app back to the

    Repository layout

    android/
  aosp/                 AOSP prebuilt, init, and SELinux integration template
  kernelsu-next/        KernelSU Next and Magisk module source

    • Port notes: Rodin Essential to Dash (MT6991)

    This tree is a port of Rodin Essential

    by NEESCHAL-3, reworked for the MediaTek MT6991 dash platform by

    afrizal1211, and carried along the SaanOS line of the same project by

    Saan. The upstream release it is based on is v1.18.5. The upstream

    project's licence, copyright notice and release history are preserved;

    NOTICE lists the modifications.

    The port is tested on real hardware by the

    @PocoX8ProMaxID Telegram community.

    The port changed the following. Every value was taken from the shipped dash

    kernel, device tree and ROM rather than carried over from MT6899.

    The GPU ladder

    The upstream target's Mali-G720 published a uniformly spaced 26 MHz

    operating-point ladder, so an OPP index could be computed from a frequency with

    a formula. Dash's Immortalis-G925 does not:

  • The device tree publishes 52 operating points from 1612 MHz down to 338 MHz,

    • and the three lowest entries all report the same 338 MHz.

  • The Mali devfreq node advertises 50 frequencies, while the GPUEB's own DVFS

    • ladder has 52 slots. The same frequency therefore sits at a different index

    in each: 598 MHz is devfreq index 39 but GPUEB index 49, and 338 MHz is

    devfreq index 49 but GPUEB index 51.

    The daemon consequently resolves every operating-point index against the ladder

    the driver publishes at /proc/gpufreqv2/gpu_working_opp_table, and it

    publishes a floor and a ceiling the way MediaTek's own tooling does:

    custom_boost_gpu_freq carries the ladder position of the requested minimum,

    custom_upbound_gpu_freq the position of the requested maximum, and the

    gpu_cust_boost_freq / gpu_cust_upbound_freq parameters carry the

    frequencies themselves. A request the ladder cannot satisfy is reported as an

    error rather than written as a guessed index, because a wrong index moves the

    floor to an unrelated frequency.

    Device baselines

    | Item | Upstream target | Dash |

    | --- | --- | --- |

    | GPU devfreq | 13000000.mali | 48000000.mali |

    | GPU ladder | 260–1300 MHz, 41 uniform steps | 338–1612 MHz, 52 uneven steps |

    | Mali cooling device | fixed cooling_device3 | resolved by type devfreq-48000000.mali |

    | UFS devfreq | 112b0000.ufshci | 16810000.ufshci |

    | DVFSRC devfreq | /devices/platform/soc/1c00f000.dvfsrc/... | /devices/platform/1c013000.dvfsrc/... |

    | Backlight | /sys/class/backlight/panel0-backlight | /sys/class/leds/lcd-backlight |

    | Native resolution | 1220 x 2712 | 1280 x 2772 |

    | Touch panel | Goodix / FocalTech | Novatek NT38771 |

    The CPU cluster layout is unchanged: Dash exposes the same 4+3+1 policy

    numbering (policy0, policy4, policy7) with eight cores.

    Thermal ownership

    Dash's thermal interface is the same one the upstream target used, including

    the thermal_message/sconfig configuration mode that suppresses the vendor's

    competing CPU policy while a custom CPU range is held. The vendor thermal

    services stay running in every mode.

    Gaming Dynamic and Extreme Beast borrow the vendor's thermal_ap configuration

    (mode MI_THERMAL_AP_MODE) instead of the thermal-nolimits mode CPU ranges

    use. The borrow is disabled by default (MI_THERMAL_AP_MODE = -1); enable it

    after on-device verification by setting the mode id. GPU thermal borrow applies

    only when no CPU range is saved — CPU range ownership holds the stricter

    nolimits mode, which takes precedence. The borrow is journaled via the

    service control journal and restored on release.

    A background guard self-heals a stuck sconfig=6 (nolimits) left by a daemon

    restart or a lost save: when no saved range or thermal mode owner exists and the

    live mode reads 6, it immediately writes 0 (normal) and logs a warning. The

    fresh-boot -1 sentinel is normalized to 0 by normalize_mi_thermal_config_mode,

    so clean boots never false-trigger.

    The platform's GPU ceiling

    Dash's ladder has a plateau. Its 24 middle slots all report 1430 MHz, so a

    1430 MHz floor resolves to the last of them and a 1430 MHz ceiling to the

    first, and both name the same clock. The MediaTek firmware's own THERMAL_EB

    row caps at the first of those slots, so the firmware's thermal ceiling is

    1430 MHz even though the ladder's top operating point is 1612 MHz.

    That ceiling cannot be raised from software. The limit table the thermal

    framework arbitrates through is read-only on this ROM, and the platform's

    power service holds the GPU at or below 1430 MHz regardless. The app

    therefore reports the cap rather than fighting it: a profile whose own writes

    landed is shown as *armed and capped by THERMAL_EB*, with the effective

    ceiling read from the driver, and it is not re-applied on every tick.

    The effective ceiling is read twice, because the driver publishes it twice:

    as an index in the power policy status dump, and directly in hertz in

    /sys/kernel/thermal/gpu_info. The second form is simpler and does not need

    the status dump to be read whole.

    Known differences

  • Dash's stock kernel publishes no bypass-charging node, so the bypass-charging

    • feature reports itself as unsupported rather than pretending to provide

    direct power. The charge-current limit is still available: dash exposes

    constant_charge_current on the battery power supply.

  • The charge-current tiers follow the upstream calibration. The absolute

    • ceiling comes from the vendor charger configuration, which is not part of the

    public ROM dump, so it should be confirmed against the target hardware; the

    daemon verifies every write against its readback and reports a clamped or

    rejected value instead of pretending it applied.
